<description>
{
 "summary": "Prevents wallet fee-bumped transactions from receiving a locktime older than the transaction they replace. When `bumpfee` creates a replacement transaction, the original transaction's locktime is passed to `DiscourageFeeSniping` as a lower bound, constraining random anti-fee-sniping backdating to the range between the previous locktime and the chain tip.",
 "problem": "Bitcoin Core's anti-fee-sniping logic randomly backdates transaction locktimes by up to 99 blocks approximately 10% of the time. When bumping fees, this random backdating can cause a replacement transaction to have an earlier locktime than the original, creating an unnatural on-chain pattern that acts as a fingerprint identifying Bitcoin Core or Electrum wallets.",
 "evidence": [
  "Closes issue #26526 ('Wallet: Don't backdate locktime rbf').",
  "PR author's empirical analysis of over 1,000,000 RBF transactions between May 2025 and June 2026 found 200-300 backdated replacements per week (<2% of all replacements), concluding that 'the few transactions that do exhibit backdating are easily fingerprintable as having been replaced using bumpfee in Bitcoin Core or Electrum.'"

<category name="wallet" title="Wallet">
## Covers

The bitcoind wallet: key and descriptor management, transaction creation
and coin selection, PSBT handling, wallet database (SQLite, and the
legacy BDB migration path), backup and recovery, rescanning, wallet RPCs,
and wallet-facing pieces of the GUI. Fee estimation is wallet when the
change is about how the wallet uses it.

Borderline: a descriptor or PSBT change that affects only `bitcoin-tx` or
RPC without wallet code is rpc, not wallet. An `interfaces::Wallet`
change is both wallet and ipc.

## What matters here

Fund safety first: anything that could lose keys, double-spend
unintentionally, create an unspendable output, or corrupt the wallet
database. Then backup, recovery, and migration correctness, including the
legacy-to-descriptor migration path that every remaining legacy user
must cross. Then privacy of transaction creation (address reuse, change
detection, fingerprinting). Then user-visible reliability: hangs, slow
rescans, confusing failures, wrong balances. Then features users have
asked for, with evidence they have asked.

The rubric does not ask whether Bitcoin Core should have a wallet. It
asks, given that it does, what a wallet user needs most.
